name: Cell Counting Calculator
seoDesc: Cell counting turns a haemocytometer count, a dilution and a suspension volume into cells per mL. Free cell counting calculator: enter your values and get con
summary:
Cell counting turns a haemocytometer count, a dilution and a suspension volume into cells per mL. It returns concentration, total cells available, volume to take and wells at 100 000 per well, and the panel shows all of them at once.

It also returns the total cells in the suspension and the volume to take for a target number of cells. Every result is derived from the boxes you fill in, so changing one input updates the whole panel at once. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Cell Counting
sections.html:
Cells/mL = (count ÷ squares) × dilution × 10⁴; volume to take = cells needed ÷ cells/mL

sections.title: How do I use the Cell Counting?
sections.html:
The form asks only for what the formula needs — nothing is optional decoration.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: cells counted of 340 cells, squares counted of 4, dilution factor of 1 ×, suspension volume of 12 mL, cells needed of 2,000,000 cells.

Substituting them into the formula gives concentration of 850,000 cells/mL, total cells available of 10,200,000 cells, volume to take of 2.35 mL, wells at 100 000 per well of 102 wells.

The arithmetic is the page's own: change one box and the result moves by the amount the formula implies, which is the quickest way to convince yourself the tool is honest.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Count twice, from two separate loadings, and average: the difference between loadings is a better error estimate than any single count.

  • Take the volume with a pipette that is appropriate for it — 20 µL out of 12 mL carries a much larger relative error than 2 mL.

  • If the count varies by more than 15% between loadings, the suspension is not homogeneous: triturate and start again.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
The arithmetic is simple; the inputs are where things go wrong. The usual culprits:

  • Using the average of counts taken from the same loading as if they were independent.
  • Forgetting that the dilution factor applies to every downstream number.
  • Seeding by volume rather than by cell number, which drifts as the culture grows.

faq.q: How precise is a haemocytometer count?
faq.a: About 10–15% between operators when 100–200 cells are counted per square.

faq.q: Should I count before or after dilution?
faq.a: Count after all dilutions and record the total factor; that is what the calculation needs.

faq.q: What does the Cell Counting actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns concentration, total cells available, volume to take and wells at 100 000 per well. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
